column6: Jehoshaphat tells the people to believe the Lord and be established, and believe his prophets and succeed; the verse puts two table roots in sequence, linking trust to a prospering outcome without proving either cognacy.

column5: Arabic خ س ر / Hebrew חסר, table sound correspondence only
column6: The righteous eats to satisfaction while the wicked person's stomach lacks; the Hebrew deficiency verb marks a concrete moral shortfall rather than a mere sad feeling.

column5: Life as a hired worker's term
column6: Job compares human days on earth to the days of a hired worker; it frames the wage longing in the next verse as a figure for mortal duration.
The wicked borrow and do not repay, while the righteous are generous and give; the commentary's mutual right is tested at the point of an outstanding debt.
The speaker commands rescue of people being taken to death; the next verse's divine weighing and repayment rests on this concrete neglected duty.
The prophet recalls a period with no wages for human or beast and no peace for travel; the absence of pay makes the coming restoration more than abstract prosperity.
The speaker's flesh and heart may fail, yet God remains his portion forever; the lasting share is opposed to the exhausted mortal self and goods.
The people are promised light if they pour themselves out for the hungry and satisfy the afflicted; the commentary's expiring personal capital is put to another's need.
The proverb calls a just balance and scales the Lord's and treats the weights as his work; fair commercial measurement belongs within divine order.
The prophet identifies wicked wealth and a deficient grain measure in the house; hoarded capital and short measure share one household.
The instruction says to remember that death will not delay; it counters the commentary's hope that a short extension will remain available.

column5: Give to a friend before death
column6: The speaker urges doing good to a friend and giving while still alive; possession can meet another's claim only before the human deadline.
Tobit tells his son almsgiving delivers from death and prevents descent into darkness; the stored treasure in the prior instruction has a concrete life-saving return.

column5: Little with righteousness exceeds unjust wealth
column6: Raphael ranks prayer and almsgiving with righteousness above riches with injustice; the scale of moral value differs from the amount in a purse.

column5: The grave does not cancel accounting
column6: The saying warns that death cannot serve as a refuge because one must give an account before the divine king; the commentary's closing day still leaves an audit.
The addressees must not store treasure where moth and rust destroy and thieves break in; this specifies how the commentary's earthly capital can disappear.

column5: Sell holdings and give poor for heavenly treasure
column6: Jesus tells a wealthy man to sell his possessions and give to the poor to have treasure in heaven; another person's need converts current capital into enduring value.

column5: Salvation described as grace through faith
column6: The letter says salvation comes by grace through faith as God's gift; it puts a gift frame beside the commentary's wage frame for believing.

column5: Not from works, so no boasting
column6: The writer explicitly excludes works as the source of salvation; this differs from any reading of the commentary's good-work wage as earned entitlement.

column5: Good works still prepared for believers
column6: The saved are described as created for good works in which to walk; it qualifies the previous gift language with a continuing place for intentional deeds.
James says Abraham's faith was active with his works and brought to completion through them; it develops the conjunction of believing and acting beyond the bare formula.
James concludes that a person is justified by works and not faith alone; it places the commentary's joined belief and work within a specific interpretive dispute.

column5: Sparing or generous sowing and reaping
column6: The measure of what one sows determines the harvest in Paul's appeal for a collection; charity is treated as an investment whose return follows its measure.
Paul says current abundance should supply others' lack and later the relationship may reverse, creating equality; the commentary's mutual rights are an exchange across time.
Paul asks what his wage is and answers that he preaches without charge rather than using his right in the gospel; refusing immediate pay itself becomes his chosen return.
The speaker says he searches minds and hearts and will give each according to works; intentional acts and the final payout are assessed together.
The one who conquers and keeps the speaker's works until the end receives authority; the reward requires continuing good action across the remaining time.
The scorching sun withers a flower, and the rich person similarly fades while pursuing business; time erodes both the trader and the expected gain.

column5: Unknown day and hour require watch
column6: The parable closes by telling hearers to watch because the day and hour are unknown; the closed door has an unknowable rather than negotiable deadline.
The teaching asks believers who share in immortal things to share even more in mortal goods and not claim these as solely their own; the commentary's passing capital carries a mutual obligation.
